items.question: What does HeatAhead do?
items.answer: HeatAhead uses weather and building history to estimate winter heating risk across New York City. Use it to check a property, explore patterns on the map, and help prioritize inspections. It is a planning tool, not a live sensor or a guarantee that heat will fail.

items.question: How can I check my building?
items.answer: Open Check a building, enter its street address or 10-digit BBL, and select Look up. Include the borough in an address. The record shows modeled risk, complaints, violations and available owner information. Use a building address only.

items.question: What is a BBL?
items.answer: A BBL is the 10-digit Borough, Block and Lot identifier used for a New York City tax lot. The first digit identifies the borough. A tax lot may contain more than one physical building. You can search by street address if you do not know its BBL.

items.question: How can I explore the risk map?
items.answer: Open the risk map to explore all five boroughs. Use the minimum-risk slider to filter properties, the area selector to move between boroughs, and Flat map or 3D view to choose the display. Zoom in to move from area hexagons to individual property markers.

items.question: What happens when I click a hexagon?
items.answer: A hexagon groups nearby properties. Clicking it opens a list of the properties inside that area, ordered by risk and respecting your current filter. Use Next to see more entries, or Zoom to these buildings to look closer. A property marker or a list link opens that specific property record.

items.question: Why are some hexagons taller?
items.answer: In the citywide 3D view, a hexagon’s height represents the combined heating complaints last season from its displayed properties. Two properties with many complaints can be taller than twenty with few complaints. Up close, gray building shapes use map-provided geometry and heights instead.

items.question: What do the map colors mean?
items.answer: The map uses a continuous pale-blue to deep-blue scale: darker blue means higher modeled winter risk. An area hexagon shows the average risk of the properties inside it; an individual marker shows that property’s risk. Height is a separate measure of past complaint volume.

items.question: What does winter risk mean?
items.answer: Winter risk is the model’s estimate for the season, based on a property’s history and building context. It is not a live reading of your heat. Different prediction windows answer different questions, so compare a seasonal estimate with seasonal estimates. Open a building’s record to see its actual displayed estimate.

items.question: How is cold-day risk different from winter risk?
items.answer: Winter risk covers a season. The cold-day estimate on a building record concerns the next freezing-day prediction window and is shown separately. A building can have substantial risk across a whole winter while having a lower estimate for a short window. The two numbers should not be treated as interchangeable.

items.question: How can I check how accurate the estimates are?
items.answer: Open a building record and expand How accurate is this number? to compare prediction bands with observed outcomes in held-out data. Calibration describes groups of similar predictions, not certainty about one property. Displayed probabilities are capped at 99%, with bands above 20% to avoid suggesting unsupported precision.

items.question: Why do some buildings have no hexagon or risk score?
items.answer: Gray buildings come from the background map. The colored layer includes only ranked properties with coordinates that match your minimum-risk filter. Other properties may be outside that set or lack matched history or coordinates. In 3D, a hexagon with zero total recorded complaints last season stays flat; switch to Flat map to see its risk color. At street level, hexagons become colored property markers. No visible overlay does not prove zero complaints, zero risk or working heat. Reset the filter or look up the property for its available record.

links.label: Open map and reset the filter

items.question: Where does the information come from?
items.answer: The project combines public NYC building, complaint, violation, ownership and boiler records with weather information. Records are joined at building or tax-lot level. Public data can be incomplete or delayed, and a reported complaint is not the same as an inspected violation or a sensor-confirmed outage.
terms: where does the information come from

items.question: What personal information does HeatAhead use?
items.answer: The map and records show building-level information, not individual tenants. Saving alerts links your registration to your verified Google email. Public owner or agent details are business-registration records. The guide does not need personal contact details; do not enter passwords, email addresses, phone numbers or unit details into it.

items.question: How can I sign up or sign in?
items.answer: Use Continue with Google on the home page. The same button handles first-time and returning users; HeatAhead does not receive your Google password. You can browse the map and building records without signing in. If the button says sign-in is being set up, account access is not available yet.

items.question: Will I stay signed in when I come back?
items.answer: Choose Keep me signed in for 30 days on this device when you use Google sign-in. Browser privacy settings or clearing cookies can end the session sooner. Sign out on a shared device. After signing in again with the same Google email, saved building registrations can be restored from your account.

items.question: How can I get cold-snap email alerts?
items.answer: Sign in with Google, choose Tenant or Landlord, enter your building’s address or BBL, confirm the email-alert checkbox and save. Alerts are designed for forecast cold spells and qualifying building risk, not every cold day. Email delivery also depends on the alert service being enabled; you can always check a building directly.

items.question: How can I stop alerts or remove a saved building?
items.answer: Sign in with the Google account used for that registration. Under Your saved buildings, select Stop alerts & remove for the property. An unsubscribe link in an alert email also leads to a confirmation step. The guide itself does not change registrations or send messages.

items.question: How can a landlord use HeatAhead?
items.answer: Look up a building, review its history and available owner or agent records, then choose I own or manage it on the building page for self-audit wording. Registering as Landlord saves alert preferences; it does not verify ownership or grant access to private tenant data.

items.question: How can I draft a message about my building?
items.answer: Open the building record, find the drafted-notice section and choose the tenant or landlord wording. Select Draft the notice, review the text, then copy it or open your email app. Nothing is automatically sent. Owner records may include a business mailing address rather than an email address.

links.label: Find a building and draft a notice

items.question: How can inspectors use the ranked queue?
items.answer: Open the live monitor to view the prioritized queue, or download the public top-500 CSV. Ranks support inspection planning; they do not confirm a violation. The Government preference on an account selects an inspector-oriented view rather than verifying employment or unlocking private records.

items.question: Is the live monitor showing events happening right now?
items.answer: The monitor demonstrates how complaints can re-sort an inspection queue through a historical replay. Use its replay clock and scoring-mode labels to understand what is running. A replay is not a live report of today’s outages. If the service is offline, the map and existing building records can still be used.

items.question: What should I do if I have no heat or hot water?
items.answer: Contact your landlord, superintendent or managing agent about the problem. If it is not resolved, use NYC311 to report a heat or hot-water problem. Give any contact and service details directly to NYC311, not this guide. Do not wait for a model score or an email alert before reporting an existing problem.

items.question: What are NYC’s heat and hot-water requirements?
items.answer: NYC heat season runs October 1–May 31. From 6 AM–10 PM, indoor temperature must reach at least 68°F when it is below 55°F outside. From 10 PM–6 AM, at least 62°F is required regardless of outdoor temperature. Hot water must reach at least 120°F year-round. See HPD for current official guidance.

sources.label: NYC HPD: heat and hot water

items.question: Are the building photos and shapes live?
items.answer: The building page offers aerial imagery and a link to the nearest available Google Street View panorama. Capture dates and coverage vary; the images are not live. The location marker identifies the mapped property point. Gray map footprints and heights provide context and are not a prediction of the building’s physical condition.

items.question: Does a high score mean a building will definitely lose heat?
items.answer: No. A risk estimate is uncertain and does not confirm an outage or violation. Complaints reflect reporting behavior as well as possible heating problems; unreported problems can be missing. Weather forecasts and public records also have limits. Use the score to plan a closer look, not to accuse an owner or dismiss a tenant’s report.

items.question: What if I smell gas or a carbon-monoxide alarm sounds?
items.answer: If you smell gas or a carbon-monoxide alarm sounds, leave the building and call 911 from outside. HeatAhead cannot dispatch help or assess an emergency. For a heating-service problem without immediate danger, use NYC311.
